Example of a clinical question, recommendation and supporting evidence 5.7 Peer review process Peer review occurs after an initial review of at least two drafts by the GC and aims to be a transparent and robust opportunity for a wide range of stakeholders to review and comment on the draft guideline. A range of stakeholder organisations and individual peer reviewers are invited to comment. Invited peer reviewers include Specialist Societies, Royal Colleges, clinicians who have published within the subject area, experts who practise in this area and relevant patient/user groups. The opportunity to comment on guidelines is advertised within regular membership communications. The draft guideline is also placed on the RCOG website in a prominent position as an open access document. This allows anyone to comment; stakeholder registration is not required. Developing a Green-top Guideline Page 18 of 27 © 2025 Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists The peer review process is not anonymous. All those peer reviewing GTGs are asked to declare any interests as part of the peer review proforma; these are published alongside the guideline as supporting information. Comments received are considered systematically. All comments are collated by the RCOG and tabulated for consideration by the guideline leads. Each comment requires a response from the developer team. Where comments are rejected, justification will need to be made. Following review of the comments, the guideline is updated and the GC will review the revised draft and the table of comments. An audit trail of the comments, amendments and various drafts is retained by RCOG staff within the guideline files. The list of peer reviewers, together with the guideline developers is included in the published guideline. 5.8 Approval Following sign-off of the post peer review draft by the GC, the draft is sent to CQAG for final quality assurance ahead of publication. Once signed off by CQAG, the Guidance team will prepare the guideline for typesetting and will request that all the guideline developers complete a declaration of interests form, which will be published alongside the guideline. chunks.content: Introduction Operative vaginal delivery (OVD) refers to a vaginal delivery in which forceps or a vacuum device are used to assist the birth [ ]. Indications for performing an OVD include a prolonged second stage of labor, evidence or risk of fetal distress, and the need to expedite delivery to assist the mother [ ]. Instrumental deliveries account for 10-15% of all births and are associated with higher maternal and neonatal morbidity, which contributes to an increased risk of litigation [ ]. Instrumental deliveries carry an increased risk of maternal and neonatal injury. Maternal complications may result in significant functional issues, such as fecal incontinence, which can have a profound impact on quality of life. Therefore, it is essential to obtain informed consent before any medical procedure [ ]. Rates of OVDs have been declining globally, with a particularly marked reduction in the use of obstetric forceps. This trend has occurred alongside rising cesarean section rates worldwide, raising concerns about the diminishing proficiency in OVD techniques as cesarean delivery (CD) becomes increasingly favored [ ]. Over the past three decades, CD rates and the incidence of associated accreta spectrum disorders have risen steadily, while the use of OVD and trials of labor after cesarean have declined. The effects of obstetric surgery on reproductive outcomes and future fertility options remain clinically significant [ ]. According to the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) Green-Top Guideline No. 26 (April 2020), it is crucial to know when to discontinue the procedure, the maximum number of attempts or pulls permitted, and the point at which the instrument should be abandoned to ensure patient safety [ ]. The safe and effective use of OVDs requires adherence to established guidelines, proper training, and continuous audit of clinical outcomes. Audit and research on OVD practices help identify gaps in clinical practice, assess compliance with guidelines, and improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the patterns, indications, and outcomes of OVDs in our institution over a specified period, providing insights into current practice and areas for quality improvement. This audit was conducted at Bedford Hospital, part of the Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust in the East of England. The audit standards were based on the RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 26 as well as local trust guidelines. Materials and methods This was a retrospective audit conducted at Bedford Hospital, part of the Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust in the East of England, over a four-month period from September to December 2024. All women who underwent attempted instrumental vaginal delivery during the study period were included, regardless of whether the procedure was successful. No specific exclusion criteria were applied. A total of 62 women met the inclusion criteria. A consecutive non-probability sampling approach was used, including all eligible cases during the audit period. Data were extracted from electronic records (Mediviewer), including maternity and delivery notes, with additional information regarding antibiotic administration and venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis (Tinzaparin) obtained from the NerveCenter system. The audit assessed adherence to specific parameters outlined in the RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 26 (April 2020) and local trust protocols. These parameters included documentation of indication for OVD, type of instrument used, number of pulls, procedural success, decision-to-delivery intervals, operator grade, consultant presence, written consent, post-procedure debriefing, administration of antibiotic prophylaxis, and completion of postnatal VTE assessment. Maternal outcomes assessed included third-degree perineal tears, estimated blood loss >1,000 mL, and massive obstetric hemorrhage. Neonatal outcomes included special care baby unit (SCBU) admission, shoulder dystocia, APGAR scores, arterial pH, and birth weight. Decision-to-delivery intervals were evaluated against standards: ≤30 minutes for cardiotocography concerns and ≤75 minutes for prolonged second stage of labor. Maternal and neonatal outcomes, documentation quality, and adherence to RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 26 and local trust guidelines were also assessed. Compliance with RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 26 and local trust guidelines was assessed for all parameters [ ]. All parameters were pre-defined to ensure that the audit could be reproduced in other settings using the same standards. Data were analyzed descriptively, with categorical variables presented as frequencies and percentages and continuous variables summarized using mean ± standard deviation where applicable. Ethical approval for the audit was granted by the Bedford Hospital audit department, and individual patient consent was not required due to the retrospective nature of the study and anonymization of data. The monthly rate of instrumental deliveries was 9/225 (4%) in September, 16/211 (7.58%) in October, 25/198 (12.6%) in November, and 12/224 (5.36%) in December. All procedures were successful, achieving a 100% (62/62) success rate. Results Between September and December 2024, 62 OVDs were performed. The monthly rate of instrumental deliveries was 9/225 (4%) in September, 16/211 (7.58%) in October, 25/198 (12.6%) in November, and 12/224 (5.36%) in December. All procedures were successful, achieving a 100% (62/62) success rate. The indication for instrumental delivery was documented in 96.77% (60/62) of cases, with only two instances not documented by the doctor but noted in the midwife’s records. The distribution of indications is illustrated in Figure , showing the proportion of cases due to delay in the second stage of labor, suspected fetal hypoxia, or both. Overall, decision-to-delivery intervals ranged from 3 to 73 minutes. Five (5/62, 8.1%) cases did not meet the recommended decision-to-delivery interval criteria. Of these, one case was delayed due to temperature issues in the theater; an alternative theater was arranged, the incident was reported, and later investigated. Another case was delayed because an instrument was initially applied but removed due to absent contractions; oxytocin was subsequently initiated, and the instrument was reapplied. For the remaining three cases, no specific cause for the delay could be identified from the documentation. Vacuum and forceps were used equally, with 29 cases each (29/62;46.8%), while sequential instruments were required in four (4/62; 6.4%) cases, as shown in Figure . Registrars performed 57 of the deliveries (57/62; 91.9%), and consultants performed five (5/62; 8.1%); a consultant was present in 22 (22/62; 35.5%) cases. Overall, 39 deliveries occurred in the delivery suite room (39/62; 62.9%), while 23 were conducted in theatre (23/62; 37.1%). All doctors performing the procedures were deemed competent. Appropriate trial of instrumental delivery was ensured in cases with occiput posterior, occiput transverse, or high head with caput/moulding. Indications for instrumental delivery were documented in 60/62 (96.8%) cases, and consent was documented in 96.8% of cases, either written (for theatre deliveries) or verbal (for delivery-suite births). The operative details, maternal outcomes, and neonatal outcomes are summarized in Table . Maternal outcomes included four third-degree perineal tears (6.45%) and estimated blood loss over 1,000 mL in eight women. Two women experienced massive obstetric hemorrhage, which is described below to highlight learning points. Case 1, with massive obstetric hemorrhage of 2,200 mL, was a 31-year-old primiparous, white British woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 25.9 kg/m² who underwent a Kiwi vacuum delivery for a full-term pregnancy at 09:05 with two pulls. The baby was born in good condition. The placenta was delivered at 09:44, but the cord snapped during controlled cord traction, and the placenta appeared incomplete. Two additional pieces of placenta were removed on vaginal examination. Despite administration of oxytocin, ergometrine, tranexamic acid, and a single dose of hemabate, bleeding continued. A code red was called at 1,000 mL estimated blood loss due to uterine atony and retained placenta. Bimanual compression was performed. Pre-delivery hemoglobin was 118 g/L, and post-delivery hemoglobin was 63 g/L; one unit of red blood cells was transfused. Surgery for manual removal of the placenta was delayed due to another ongoing emergency and consent process. Surgery was performed in the theater under spinal anesthesia at 11:32. She recovered well, but no debrief or senior review was documented. Learning point from this case was to escalate promptly to the consultant and matron on call. Case 2, with massive obstetric hemorrhage of 1,940 mL, was a 30-year-old primiparous woman with a BMI of kg/m² who underwent a forceps delivery with episiotomy at 17:51 due to fetal tachycardia. Two pulls were performed in the delivery room, and the baby was born in good condition. Postpartum hemorrhage was both traumatic and atonic. Management included oxytocin bolus, ergometrine, tranexamic acid, and one dose of hemabate. Episiotomy suturing was completed at 18:24, and bleeding was brought under control. Learning point from this case was to improve monitoring of estimated blood loss, escalate promptly, initiate a massive obstetric hemorrhage call, and document debrief. Sequential instruments were successfully used in four women, with only one neonate requiring SCBU admission. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered in 70.9% of women, while postnatal VTE assessments were completed in 90%. Debriefing was documented in only 16% of cases. Neonatal outcomes were favorable overall. Two babies were admitted to the SCBU, four experienced shoulder dystocia, and one had an APGAR score <5 at birth, while another had an APGAR score <7 at five minutes. Three babies had an arterial pH <7.10, and eight had a birth weight above 4 kg. The maximum pulls recorded were four, with only one case requiring four pulls using a Kiwi vacuum. Patient demographics showed 47 primiparous women (47/62; 75.8%), 11 para 1 (11/62; 17.7%), 3 para 2 (3/62; 4.8%), and 1 para 3 (1/62; 1.6%). The majority (45)

Two babies were admitted to the SCBU, four experienced shoulder dystocia, and one had an APGAR score <5 at birth, while another had an APGAR score <7 at five minutes. Three babies had an arterial pH <7.10, and eight had a birth weight above 4 kg. The maximum pulls recorded were four, with only one case requiring four pulls using a Kiwi vacuum. Patient demographics showed 47 primiparous women (47/62; 75.8%), 11 para 1 (11/62; 17.7%), 3 para 2 (3/62; 4.8%), and 1 para 3 (1/62; 1.6%). The majority (45) had gestational ages between 37 and 41 weeks, nine between 34 and 37 weeks, and eight between 41 and 42 weeks. BMI distribution included three women <20 kg/m², 25 women 20-25 kg/m², 26 women 26-30 kg/m², and 11 women >30 kg/m². Induction of labor was performed in 26 (26/62; 41.9%) women, with the remaining 36 undergoing spontaneous onset of labor (36/62; 58.1%). Analgesia was appropriately provided in all cases, with 29 women receiving Entonox (29/62; 46.8%) and 10 receiving pethidine (10/62; 16.1%). Patient demographics and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table . Overall, the audit demonstrated that OVDs in this cohort were conducted safely with high success rates and appropriate indications. Areas for improvement included documentation of debriefing, postnatal VTE assessment completion, and ensuring antibiotic prophylaxis adherence. The two massive obstetric hemorrhage cases emphasize the importance of timely escalation, senior review, and structured debriefing to optimize patient safety. Discussion This audit reviewed 62 OVDs over a four-month period. The overall rate of instrumental deliveries ranged from 4% to 12.6% monthly, which aligns with national and international reports indicating rates ranging between 5% and 15% depending on the obstetric population and institutional practice [ , ]. The 100% procedural success rate demonstrates safe and effective practice, consistent with studies showing that with proper training, OVDs can be performed with high success and low morbidity [ ]. This aligns with recent studies indicating high success rates for vacuum-assisted deliveries, with one study reporting a 97.3% success rate for vacuum attempts [ ]. Documentation of indications and consent was achieved in most cases (96.77% and 92%, respectively), although this remains similar to the previous audit, indicating persistent gaps in record-keeping. A recent study highlighted that documentation compliance remains a challenge, with many OVDs lacking complete documentation, including indications and consent [ ]. This underscores the need for standardized documentation practices to enhance clinical accountability and communication. Compliance with decision-to-delivery intervals was comparable to the previous audit (92% versus 93%), which is in line with current guidelines recommending timely intervention in second-stage complications [ ]. Maternal outcomes were largely favorable, with low rates of third-degree perineal tears (6.45%), and most patients experienced manageable blood loss. While two cases of massive obstetric hemorrhage were observed, it is important to note that these are recognized complications that can also occur in spontaneous vaginal deliveries. Therefore, these events cannot be attributed solely to the use of instruments but highlight the importance of prompt escalation, senior review, and structured debriefing, as recommended in national guidelines for the management of postpartum hemorrhage [ ]. Recent guidelines emphasize the use of a treatment bundle for the management of postpartum hemorrhage, which was followed in these cases, including uterotonics, tranexamic acid, and escalation of care if bleeding persists [ ]. Sequential instruments were used safely in four women, all resulting in successful deliveries, demonstrating that complex operative techniques can be performed effectively with appropriate supervision [ ]. This is consistent with recent studies indicating that when performed by trained professionals, sequential instrument deliveries can be safe and effective [ ]. Neonatal outcomes were reassuring, with minimal need for SCBU admission and isolated cases of low APGAR scores or shoulder dystocia. These findings are consistent with previous studies indicating that OVD, when appropriately indicated and performed by trained staff, is generally safe for the neonate [ , ]. Areas for improvement identified include post-procedure debriefing (documented in only 16%), completion of postnatal VTE assessment (90%), antibiotic prophylaxis adherence (70.9%), and paired cord gas collection (77.4%). Addressing these gaps aligns with best-practice recommendations and will further enhance patient safety and quality of care. Recommendations Based on the findings of this audit, several measures are recommended to improve the safety and quality of OVDs. Implement the use of a delivery categorization sticker to classify deliveries, operative vaginal or cesarean, based on urgency (Category 1 or 2) and indicate the recommended location (delivery suite room or theatre). This tool will support timely decision-making, ensure appropriate escalation of care, and improve adherence to recommended decision-to-delivery intervals in line with RCOG guidelines. Recommendations Based on the findings of this audit, several measures are recommended to improve the safety and quality of OVDs. Implement the use of a delivery categorization sticker to classify deliveries, operative vaginal or cesarean, based on urgency (Category 1 or 2) and indicate the recommended location (delivery suite room or theatre). This tool will support timely decision-making, ensure appropriate escalation of care, and improve adherence to recommended decision-to-delivery intervals in line with RCOG guidelines. Although the sticker is copyright-protected and cannot be shared externally, its implementation is intended to further enhance compliance with guidelines and support quality improvement in future audits. The delivery categorization sticker has been implemented to improve decision-making and adherence to decision-to-delivery intervals. A standardized documentation template should be developed to capture essential details, including in-room consent, a clear indication for the procedure, and a structured post-procedure debrief, which will help address persistent gaps in record-keeping. Antibiotic prophylaxis should be administered consistently as a single dose post-delivery when indicated, and paired cord gases should be collected for all babies to ensure comprehensive neonatal assessment and documentation. Re-audit in six months is recommended to evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions and monitor ongoing compliance with best practice standards. Limitations This audit has a few limitations. As it was conducted at a single center, the findings may not apply to other hospitals. Only short-term maternal and neonatal outcomes were assessed, and no long-term follow-up was performed. It is important to note that the primary aim of this audit was to evaluate adherence to guidelines and recommendations for OVDs, including documentation, decision-to-delivery intervals, and immediate procedural outcomes. Long-term follow-up of women who sustained obstetric anal sphincter injuries was not within the scope of this audit, but can be explored in a separate prospective study focusing on maternal recovery and patient perceptions after OVD. Conclusions This audit demonstrated that OVDs in this cohort were performed safely, with high success rates and appropriate indications. Maternal and neonatal outcomes were generally favorable, including in cases requiring sequential instruments. However, rare but significant complications, such as massive obstetric hemorrhage, underscore the importance of timely escalation, senior review, and structured debriefing. Focused efforts on improving documentation, adherence to post-delivery protocols, and systematic monitoring will help maintain and further enhance the quality of care.

chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION Macrosomia, defined as neonatal birth weight ≥4000 g, is a condition that occurs in approximately 3.9% of all deliveries, and poses substantial obstetric challenges. The prevalence of macrosomia is influenced by several factors, including pre‐gestational diabetes and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), previous macrosomic infant, maternal obesity, excessive weight gain during pregnancy and advanced maternal age. , , , , Macrosomia is associated with an increased risk for maternal complications including cesarean delivery (CD), prolonged labor and labor dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) and severe perineal lacerations, , , while the offsprings faces an increased risk for shoulder dystocia, Erb's palsy, hypoglycemia, hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and neonatal mortality. , , Nulliparous, defined as women those who have never delivered, encounter distinct subgroup of parturients, with generally higher risk for adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes , compared to multiparous women (women who delivered before). The rate of interventions such as CD, and vacuum assisted deliveries is substantially higher in nulliparous even without any additional risk. Also, there is an increased risk of adverse maternal outcomes (infection, severe perineal lacerations, thromboembolism and the need for blood transfusions) and adverse neonatal outcomes, even perinatal mortality. Despite extensive literature on macrosomia and nulliparity as independent risk factors for adverse obstetric outcomes, data on the specific combination of these two conditions is scant. Existing studies have primarily compared nulliparous and multiparous women with macrosomic neonates, focusing largely on CD rates , Others have relied on estimated fetal weight rather than actual birth weight, limiting their accuracy. Furthermore, many studies have not stratified outcomes by parity, thereby obscuring potential differences unique to nulliparous women. Given that gap, our study aimed to determine whether macrosomia is associated with increased intrapartum CD among nulliparous women, as well as other adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. 2 MATERIALS AND METHODS 2.1 Study design A multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from two university‐affiliated medical centers in Jerusalem, Israel: Shaare Zedek Medical Center (SZMC) and Bikur Holim Medical Center (BHMC), that accounted for approximately 16% of all deliveries in Israel, averaging 22 000 births annually. Demographic, obstetric, and delivery‐related data were extracted from electronic medical records to minimize recall and reporting bias inherent to retrospective designs. The study period spans deliveries occurring between 2005 and 2024. 2.2 Study population The study included all women in first delivery (nulliparous) with singleton, viable pregnancy, who delivered at term (37–42 weeks of gestation) at our medical centers during the study period. We compared women with macrosomic neonates (4000 g or greater) to a reference group of women with neonates weighted 3000–3500 g. We excluded multiparous women, women with multiple pregnancies, preterm deliveries, elective CDs, pre‐labor fetal demise, lethal fetal anomaly, or known genetic abnormality. We also made a subanalysis that examined the association between maternal and neonatal outcomes according to six different groups of neonatal birth weights. 2.3 Ethical considerations The study was approved by the SZMC Institutional Review Board (IRB no. 0029‐25 SZMC‐0055‐25) which oversees research at both medical centers. Informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study and the use of de‐identified data, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. 2.4 Study outcomes The primary outcome was intrapartum cesarean delivery. Secondary outcomes included other maternal and neonatal outcomes. Secondary maternal outcomes Labor induction, gestational age at delivery, prolonged labor, prolonged second stage of labor, persistent occipito‐posterior presentation, chorioamnionitis, shoulder dystocia, episiotomy, 3–4‐degree perineal lacerations, PPH (estimated blood loss exceeding 1000 mL), blood product transfusion, prolonged maternal hospitalization, puerperal fever and maternal intensive care unit (ICU) admission. Secondary neonatal outcomes Five‐minute Apgar score <7, NICU admission, transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), mechanical ventilation, meconium aspiration, neonatal hypoglycemia, seizures, encephalopathy, intracranial hemorrhage, Erb's palsy, clavicular fracture, jaundice, sepsis, birth asphyxia and perinatal death. 2.5 Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software (version 25; IBM Corporation, Armonk, New York). Descriptive statistics summarized categorical and continuous variables. Comparisons between groups were performed using chi‐square or Fisher exact tests for categorical variables, and student's t ‐test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, depending on normality. Univariate analyses were used to evaluate associations between macrosomia in nulliparous and demographic, obstetric, and delivery characteristics. Variables found to be significant in univariate analyses were included in multivariable logistic regression models to assess independent associations between macrosomia and study outcomes. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. A two‐sided P value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Study population We had 100 422 deliveries of primiparous during the study period in our centers. After excluding 13 621 women due to preterm deliveries, multifetal gestation, antepartum fetal death, elective CDs, out of hospital deliveries and missing data, the final analytical cohort included 86 801 women. Of those women, 2762 (3.2%) delivered macrosomic neonates (birth

in univariate analyses were included in multivariable logistic regression models to assess independent associations between macrosomia and study outcomes. Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. A two‐sided P value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Study population We had 100 422 deliveries of primiparous during the study period in our centers. After excluding 13 621 women due to preterm deliveries, multifetal gestation, antepartum fetal death, elective CDs, out of hospital deliveries and missing data, the final analytical cohort included 86 801 women. Of those women, 2762 (3.2%) delivered macrosomic neonates (birth weight >4000 g), while 40 963 (47.2%) delivered neonates weighing 3000–3500 g and served as the reference group (Figure ). 3.2 Maternal and pregnancy characteristics Demographic and obstetric characteristics of the study groups are presented in Table . Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups in terms of maternal age, fertility treatment, and hypertensive disorders. However, compared to the reference group, women in the macrosomia group had significant higher rates of pre‐gestational diabetes (0.9% vs. 0.4%, P < 0.01) and obesity (18.8% vs. 10.2%, P < 0.01). They also had a mean longer gestation (40.4 ± 1.0 vs. 39.6 ± 1.1 weeks, P < 0.01), were more likely to deliver after 41 weeks (43.2% vs. 19.2%, P < 0.01), and had higher rates of labor induction (22% vs. 15.8%, P < 0.01). 3.3 Labor characteristics Women in the macrosomia group underwent more vaginal examinations (13.2 ± 13.6 vs. 11.1 ± 13, P < 0.01) and had higher rates of oxytocin augmentation (65.2% vs. 58.1%, P < 0.01). The duration of both the first and second stages of labor was significantly longer (both P < 0.01). Epidural analgesia and chorioamnionitis were also more common among the macrosomia group (78.1% vs. 72.5% and 10% vs. 4.5%, respectively, P < 0.01) (Table ). 3.4 Primary outcome The rate of intrapartum CD was significantly higher in the macrosomia group (18.6% vs. 7.8%, P < 0.01), with an aOR of 1.81 (95% CI: 0.91–3.58), as presented in Tables and . 3.5 Secondary maternal outcomes Macrosomia was associated with higher rates of second‐stage CD (7.8% vs. 2.1%, P < 0.01), failed vacuum delivery (1% vs. 0.5%, P < 0.01), and prolonged hospitalization (2.1% vs. 1%, P < 0.01). Rates of perineal trauma were significantly higher, including perineal 3–4‐degree tears (2% vs. 0.9%, P < 0.01), and episiotomy (41.7% vs. 34.9%, P < 0.01). Shoulder dystocia occurred in 2% of macrosomic deliveries compared to 0.1% in the reference group (95% CI: 11.32–98.68). PPH was significantly more common (23.5% vs. 11.3%, P < 0.01), with an increased hemoglobin drop, and higher blood product transfusion. Rates of puerperal fever were also higher (5.1% vs. 2.9%, P < 0.01) (Table ). These trends are corroborated in Figure , which showed a sharp rise in adverse maternal outcomes with increasing birth weight, particularly intrapartum CD, PPH, and blood product transfusion, peaking in neonates weighing >4500 g. 3.6 Secondary neonatal outcomes Macrosomic neonates had significantly higher rates of NICU admission (3.3% vs. 2%, P < 0.01), transient tachypnea of the newborn (2.1% vs. 1.4%, P = 0.01), mechanical ventilation (1.2% vs. 0.5%, P < 0.01), and hypoglycemia (3.3% vs. 1.8%, P < 0.01). Erb's palsy and clavicle fractures occurred more frequently (1% vs. 0.4%, P < 0.01), while the incidence of birth asphyxia was also elevated (0.5% vs. 0.3%, P = 0.01). Rates of low 5‐min Apgar scores (<7) were comparable between groups (1% vs. 0.9%, P = 0.49) (Table ). As illustrated in Figure , NICU admissions and hypoglycemia followed a U‐shaped distribution, being higher at both extremes of birth weight (<2500 and >4500 g), while shoulder dystocia and birth trauma showed a marked increase with rising birth weight. 3.7 Multivariable analysis Multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the independent association between macrosomia and adverse neonatal outcomes, adjusting for potential confounders (Table ). Macrosomia was not independently associated with the primary outcome—intrapartum CD (aOR 1.81, 95% CI: 0.91–3.58). However, it was independently associated with higher odds of shoulder dystocia (aOR 33.42, 95% CI: 11.32–98.68), PPH (aOR 2.13, 95% CI: 1.79–2.54), blood products transfusion (aOR 2.45, 95% CI: 1.51–3.98), chorioamnionitis (aOR 2.03, 95% CI: 1.57–2.61), NICU admission (aOR 1.62, 95% CI: 1.15–2.29), Erb's palsy/fracture of clavicle (aOR 9.43, 95% CI: 4.01–22.21), and neonatal hypoglycemia (aOR 2.23, 95% CI: 1.32–3.77). 4 DISCUSSION 4.1 Principal findings In this large retrospective cohort study of nulliparous women, macrosomia was associated with a significantly increased risk of intrapartum DC, compared to a reference group of neonatal birth weight 3000–3499 g. It was also associated with an increased risk of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes including PPH, 3–4‐degree perineal tear, shoulder dystocia, NICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and neonatal hypoglycemia. These findings remained significant after adjusting for relevant confounders.

It was also associated with an increased risk of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes including PPH, 3–4‐degree perineal tear, shoulder dystocia, NICU admission, mechanical ventilation, and neonatal hypoglycemia. These findings remained significant after adjusting for relevant confounders. Notably, the study demonstrated that even among nulliparous women—a group already at increased obstetric risk—macrosomia further exacerbates the likelihood of adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. While most outcomes were worsened in the macrosomia group, the incidence of low 5‐min Apgar scores did not differ significantly between groups. Additionally, in a secondary analysis that stratified outcomes by neonatal birth weight, we found a rise in adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes with increasing birth weight, particularly intrapartum CD, PPH, blood product transfusion, shoulder dystocia and birth trauma, peaking in neonates weighing >4500 g. NICU admissions and hypoglycemia followed a U‐shaped distribution, being higher at both extremes of birth weight (<2500 and >4500 g). 4.2 Results in the context of what is known Previous studies have already shown that macrosomia is a risk factor for obstetrical complications; however, most have not differed between nulliparous or multiparous women. Weissmann‐Brenner et al. reported an increased risk of CD, PPH, and neonatal complications in macrosomic pregnancies and Beta et al. in a meta‐analysis have also found an association to an increased risk of emergency CD, PPH and shoulder dystocia. Chen and Chauhan conducted a large retrospective study that compared maternal and neonatal outcome according to neonatal birth weight categories (2500–3999, 4000–4449, and 4500–5999 g). The study demonstrated that both composite maternal outcomes (including PPH and severe perineal lacerations) and composite neonatal outcome (such as birth trauma and hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy) were significantly increased in the macrosomic groups. However, in all those studies the population included both nulliparous and multiparous women. The lack of parity stratification represents a methodological limitation as it precludes assessment of risk differences between nulliparous and multiparous women. Several studies have reported that nulliparous women are at increased risk for a range of obstetrical complications compared to multiparous women, , including substantially higher risk of operative vaginal delivery, CD, anal sphincter injury, , as well as higher rates of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (including pre‐eclampsia), PPH, postpartum infections, venous thromboembolism and maternal death. , While their offspring faces an increased risk of neonatal complications such as lower neonatal Apgar scores, composite adverse neonatal outcomes (that include ventilator support or cardiopulmonary resuscitation, seizure, hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy, NEC and sepsis), , and even perinatal mortality. Therefore, it seems that some of the complications of macrosomia and nulliparous overlap, but data regarding the combined situation of nulliparity and macrosomia is scant. The several studies that exist regarding this issue did not compare nulliparous with macrosomic neonates and nulliparous with non‐macrosomic neonates. Thubert et al. found higher rates of 3–4‐degree perineal tear among deliveries of macrosomic neonates and among nulliparous women, but the combined risk of both exposures was not specifically analyzed. Larad et al. and Hehir et al. demonstrated that the rate of CD is substantially higher among nulliparous with macrosomic neonates compared to multiparous with macrosomic neonates, but they did not study other obstetrical complications and they did not compare to nulliparous that delivered neonates with normal weight. Cooley et al. suggested that macrosomia in nulliparous increases the risk of CD, but this study relied only on predelivery sonographic evaluation and not actual weight, so it is inaccurate. Levin et al. found that among nulliparous with macrosomic neonates, vaginal delivery was associated with higher maternal morbidity, while CD reduced neonatal trauma. However, this study was made on a small cohort and only examined extreme macrosomia (>4500 g). Our findings support this dual‐risk dynamic and reinforce the difficulty of optimal delivery planning for macrosomic neonates, especially in nulliparous, where decision thresholds may differ due to unproven pelvic capacity. However, the uniqueness of our study is by focusing specifically on the intersection of nulliparity and macrosomia in a very large cohort and by examining a wide range of outcomes. We compared nulliparous with macrosomic neonates to nulliparous with normal weighted neonates. Hence, we were able to demonstrate the risks compound specifically in this population. In addition, we performed a stratification by neonatal birth weight categories to further delineate how increasing neonatal birth weight impacts outcomes within nulliparous women. While previous studies have stratified outcomes by neonatal birth weight in general parturients population, , to our knowledge, none have specifically applied this stratification to first deliveries (nulliparous women) as

specifically on the intersection of nulliparity and macrosomia in a very large cohort and by examining a wide range of outcomes. We compared nulliparous with macrosomic neonates to nulliparous with normal weighted neonates. Hence, we were able to demonstrate the risks compound specifically in this population. In addition, we performed a stratification by neonatal birth weight categories to further delineate how increasing neonatal birth weight impacts outcomes within nulliparous women. While previous studies have stratified outcomes by neonatal birth weight in general parturients population, , to our knowledge, none have specifically applied this stratification to first deliveries (nulliparous women) as we have. Our approach, therefore, provides novel insight into how increasing neonatal birth weight further compounds risk in this already vulnerable group. 4.3 Clinical implications Our findings confirm that risks associated with fetal overgrowth are compounded in the setting of nulliparous women with a non‐labor‐tested pelvis, supporting a more cautious clinical approach in this subgroup. Identifying risk factors for macrosomia, such as maternal obesity, diabetes, and excessive gestational weight gain, is crucial, especially in this subpopulation. Early detection through prenatal screening and monitoring fetal growth can inform delivery planning and reduce the incidence of adverse outcomes. Multidisciplinary approaches involving obstetricians, midwives, and neonatologists are vital to optimizing care for both mother and neonate. 4.4 Research implications The optimal timing and mode of delivery in nulliparous women with suspected macrosomia is a key question that warrants further investigation. Although early induction is acceptable to mitigate the risks associated with macrosomia, evidence is inconclusive. , Further studies are needed to examine whether this intervention reduce complications of macrosomia, specifically in nulliparous women. In addition, there are no well‐defined guidelines for the best mode of delivery—CD or vaginal delivery in this subpopulation. Therefore, predictive models incorporating maternal characteristics and estimated fetal weight should be developed and validated for use in clinical decision making. Future research should also assess long‐term neonatal and maternal outcomes, including pelvic floor function and neurodevelopmental trajectories, to better understand the full impact of macrosomia in nulliparous. 4.5 Strengths and limitations The main strength of this study is the large, well‐defined cohort of nulliparous women, enabling precise estimates a wide range of complication that are associated with macrosomia. The use of actual birth weight rather than estimated fetal weight enhances the accuracy of the result and its clinical relevance. Additionally, the multivariable analysis we performed to adjust for potential confounders (such as obesity, diabetes, induction of labor and gestational age), strengthens the validity of the associations results. However, this study had several limitations. First, its retrospective design with the inherent limits of missing data and potential bias, although the use of a robust electronic medical record system likely mitigates this risk. Moreover, the lack of data on prenatal suspicion of macrosomia limits the ability to assess how antenatal decision making may have influenced outcomes. Second, as the analysis was made on data from a single tertiary center, the findings may not be generalizable to all populations, particularly given the unique demographic and cultural characteristics of our institution (high percentage of religious women who desire big families and natural approach and avoiding CD as much as possible). Finally, while key confounders were adjusted for, residual confounding by unmeasured factors cannot be excluded. 5 CONCLUSION In nulliparous women delivering at term, macrosomia is independently associated with a higher risk of intrapartum CD, high degree perineal tear, PPH, and adverse neonatal outcomes. This association underscores the importance of vigilance and careful management in labor planning, and postpartum surveillance in this vulnerable subgroup. Proactive management strategies might help mitigate risks, ensure safer deliveries, and improve maternal and neonatal outcomes. Further research is needed to guide evidence‐based interventions. Gunaratne, MBBS; Eniola R. Ibirogba, MBBS; Ayssa Teles A. Trad, MD; Amro Elrefaei, MBBCh; Regan N. Theiler, MD, PhD; Rodrigo Ruano, MD, PhD; Linda M. Szymanski, MD, PhD; Rana Chakraborty, MD, DPhil; and Vesna D. Garovic, MD, PhD Abstract The global pandemic of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the cause of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), has been associated with worse outcomes in several patient populations, including the elderly and those with chronic comorbidities. Data from previous pan- demics and seasonal inﬂuenza suggest that pregnant women may be at increased risk for infection- associated morbidity and mortality. Physiologic changes in normal pregnancy and metabolic and vascular changes in high-risk pregnancies may affect the pathogenesis or exacerbate the clinical presentation of COVID-19. Speciﬁcally, SARS-CoV-2 enters the cell via the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor, which is upregulated in normal pregnancy. Upregulation of ACE2 mediates conversion of angiotensin II (vasoconstrictor) to angiotensin-(1-7) (vasodilator) and con- tributes to relatively low blood pressures, despite upregulation of other components of the renin- angiotensin-aldosterone system. As a result of higher ACE2 expression, pregnant women may be at elevated risk for complications from SARS-CoV-2 infection. Upon binding to ACE2, SARS-CoV-2 causes its downregulation, thus lowering angiotensin-(1-7) levels, which can mimic/worsen the vasoconstriction, inﬂammation, and pro-coagulopathic effects that occur in preeclampsia. Indeed, early reports suggest that, among other adverse outcomes, preeclampsia may be more common in pregnant women with COVID-19. Medical therapy, during pregnancy and breastfeeding, relies on medications with proven safety, but safety data are often missing for medications in the early stages of clinical trials. documents.title: RCOG Male and Female Sterilisation Evidence-Based Clinical Guideline

chunks.content: Sterilisation counselling: a role for the gynaecology nurse-practitioner. A recent publication of an evidence-based clinical guideline for male and female sterilisation by the Royal College of Obstetrics and Gynaecology (RCOG) created a stimulus for a review of our female sterilisation service. We arranged for a gynaecology nurse-practitioner (A.O.) with extensive experience in general gynaecology and contraception to undergo additional training in counselling female sterilisation. She then took over the daily running of the sterilisation clinic using a care pathway and pre-printed letters. She had open access to a consultant (R.F.) for advice. A review of 100 consecutive referrals showed that the nurse followed the guidelines extremely closely both in terms of referral to the medical team for advice and/or further counselling and quality of documentation. A total of 59% of the women attending the clinic were cared for by the nurse-practitioner alone. Only four had to see a consultant. All women questioned expressed very positive comments about the style and content of counselling and just one stated she preferred to see a doctor.

documents.title: RCOG Green-top Guideline 55 Late Intrauterine Fetal Death and Stillbirth

chunks.content: An audit of healthcare professionals' knowledge regarding perinatal autopsy. Perinatal autopsy is one the most valuable investigations to ascertain the cause of death (Nijkamp et al., Seminars in Fetal & Neonatal Medicine. 22:167-175, 2017; Korteweg et al., AJOG 53, e1-12, 2012; Late Interuterine Death and Stillbirth' RCOG Green-top Guideline No.55, 2015). Discussions about perinatal autopsy can be difficult for parents and healthcare professionals. Perinatal staff need a good level of knowledge and understanding regarding perinatal autopsy in order to discuss the procedure with parents. This study aims to investigate healthcare professionals' knowledge regarding perinatal autopsy. An audit conducted in a large teaching hospital using a questionnaire was developed and distributed to healthcare professionals in the hospital. Seventy healthcare professionals participated in the audit. Of those surveyed, 64% (n = 45) have discussed perinatal autopsy with a mother and the majority of healthcare professionals (67%) found this difficult. Self-reported levels of understanding were found to be low with just 10% reporting 'excellent understanding'. The results of this audit highlight the need for further education among all healthcare professionals working with bereaved families.

documents.title: RCOG Maternal Cardiac Arrest Guidance

chunks.content: Conditions triggering local incident reviews in UK hospital maternity units: A national survey. In countries, such as the UK, where maternal deaths are rare, reviews of other severe complications of pregnancy and the puerperium can provide an additional perspective to help learn lessons to improve future care. The objective of this survey was to identify the types of incidents which triggered local reviews in the UK, in order to inform national safety reporting guidance. A national descriptive survey. UK. Consultant-led maternity units. Seventy-one per cent of maternity units provided an incident review trigger list. The conditions included were classified by two assessors. Incidents that were listed by at least 5% of maternity units were reported and compared with incidents recommended for review by the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG). The conditions covered were highly variable, although those recommended by the RCOG were most highly represented. The most commonly listed conditions that had not been recommended for review by the RCOG included inadequate staffing levels (70%), cardiac arrest (69%) and maternal sepsis (64%). Substantial variation exists in the types of incident listed for review by maternity units in the UK. Importantly, some units are not reviewing cases of severe infective complications even though this is a current major concern. Future guidance concerning local serious incident review processes should include how the list of conditions triggering a review should be managed in the light of changing clinical and safety priorities.
